of this important branch of the defence services, and particularly with regard to yie numbers to be going into camp this year. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, speaking
generally, I am advised by my officials, and I have confirmed some of this advice at first hand by observation myself, the reorganization which followed the intensive examination throughout the country of the militia system by the committee to which the hon. member has referred has resulted in very considerable improvement in the quality of militia training. I understand the equipment which has been issued has also greatly improved. The camp training has certainly improved in quality and in numbers. If I recollect correctly, in 1954, 16,000 attended summer camp; in 1955, approximately 20,000. This year there are approximately 23,000. The strength is down slightly. I have not the figures before me at the moment but it is down very little. I am told that the number of active members in the militia is really up. In other words, there was some internal reorganization. The elimination of what might be termed nominal members of the militia will improve the quality, because the only members of the militia who will profit from the reorganization or from the training are those who are actively interested. I understand further, as regards the arrangements which were made with respect to pay, the arrangements to give assistance in public relations and the arrangements to take care of a good deal of the staff work locally, and generally all the other matters that were dealt with by the committee, while each of which in itself may not be important, their cumulative effect has been such that there is a better training standard, a better feeling and a much greater activity within the militia.
We are trying to improve their equipment as fast as we can, and generally speaking I would say that the appointment of this commission was well worth while. In regard to the numbers of people participating in militia training under present conditions today, we must remember that we are in a very active industrial period. There is a high level of employment, and notwithstanding the inducements that are offered and the benefits of the training, it requires some determination on the part of individuals to devote the time and the energy, which they do, to the carrying out of their duties as members of the militia.

Last night the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich gave us a very interesting report, and he made a few suggestions that I think should be emphasized before we pass on to some other item. May I say in passing that when the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the Minister of Labour went to London recently I checked the Parliamentary Guide to And out, if I could, something about the gallantry for which the hon. members received one of the most prized awards in the commonwealth. I find that both are very modest. No mention whatever is made of the gallantry, but I am sure members on all sides of the house are
Supply-National Defence very proud to have some association with these distinguished holders of the Victoria Cross.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich mentioned, when he spoke earlier on the defence estimates, that it seemed to be extremely unlikely that either the west or the Soviet union will use thermonuclear weapons with the idea of carrying out strategic bombing either in the west or in the east. Both sides seem to have reached the realization that the use of that terrible weapon means the destruction of civilization.
In the next paragraph he said, as reported at page 6206 of Hansard:
A few years ago there was the feeling that the Russians might not use the thermonuclear weapons but might start a war in western Europe and use conventional arms. For that reason the commanders of NATO-this government, supported by this side of the house, agreed-were able to provide a strong deterrent of ground troops in western Europe.
I think conditions are changing. Not only does it appear that Russia is changing the emphasis from a war of arms to an economic war,-
Later in another paragraph he went on to say:
I feel that in the light of the changed circumstances It is imperative that this government review its defence policy. The emphasis is being changed from a war of arms to a war of trade. Whilst it is essential that we keep up defences in this country and in western Europe, I feel that we have to be quite certain that we are not overinsuring at the present time.
I think the suggestions made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich have not received sufficient consideration by the Minister of National Defence. In this morning's paper we read that the United States has withdrawn its offer to help Egypt to build the dam. It seems to me the western nations are not facing up to the real challenge that the U.S.S.R. is presenting to the world at the present time. In the mail this morning I received a pamphlet entitled, "Education and Professional Manpower in the U.S.S.R." I gather this has been sent to all hon. members. It is a reprint from "Chemistry in Canada", written by Dr. Garnet T. Page, general manager of the Chemical Institute of Canada. This presents some information that I think has not received sufficient consideration in Canada. There is a picture of the university in Moscow. It gives tables describing the courses for different fields of engineering in Russia, a typical Soviet curriculum in chemical engineering and chemistry, and then it gives tables for Canada, the United States and western Europe.
I have not had time to study these tables at all but it seems to me that since Russia is spending so much of her gross national

Supply-National Defence product in the field of training scientists and engineers we should take careful note of the words of Dr. Page. In one paragraph he says:
The Soviet educational system has been developed into a major arm for ideological and economic world conquest. Thousands of well-trained and politically indoctrinated engineers, scientists, teachers and technicians are being produced for export, to assist in developing the resources of countries outside the present Soviet orbit; and hundreds of thousands more are being prepared to meet domestic industrial needs.
When Mr. James S. Duncan, president of Massey-Harris, spoke to the Canadian Club a few weeks ago he pointed out this challenge. I have a copy of the press release in which he described the new university in Moscow which is situated on 1,100 acres of land on the banks of the Moskva river, and he describes the facilities. According to Mr. Duncan these are the most extravagant university buildings anywhere in the world. He goes on to point out that in 1954 Russia graduated almost 53,000 engineers compared to 23,000 in the United States. These students on graduation, he indicates, had put in 50 per cent more study hours than our students here. It seems to me that poses a challenge which we are not considering as we should.
The minister last night gave us the total amount it is costing us each year to maintain our forces in Germany and if you add on the total amount we spent for the planes that were recently given it seems to me that represents a very large investment. As Dr. Page points out, I think we are falling behind in Canada in the training of sufficient numbers of engineers and scientists and in making them available in our country and others that require the technical know-how we have available.
I read in the newspapers that last winter the Department of Labour called a meeting of all responsible agencies to look at this problem. I wonder if the minister could make any report to the committee as to what conclusions, if any, were reached by the advisory council or the interdepartmental committee that was established to consider whether or not we are graduating sufficient engineers and scientists in Canada to meet our own needs and to meet the challenge that Russia is presenting to the world today.
I would think that if the Minister of National Defence is able to have all the funds he needs, and without any question he has been able to do that, the suggestions made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich last night should be given the most careful scrutiny. If the best authorities are now coming to the conclusion that neither


the west nor the east is going to start a thermonuclear war and that the Canadians are not going to be required in Europe indefinitely, it seems to me more consideration should be given to seeing that Canada will not be handicapped in the years to come by having insufficient engineers and scientists to staff our high schools and universities.
Could the minister give us some report on the progress of the advisory council on professional manpower?

No, Mr. Chairman. I, too, was very pleased to hear some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich last evening. In one case he referred particularly to the excellent food the overseas brigade was receiving. It came to me as somewhat of a surprise to read an article in the Hamilton Spectator of July 12 written by a well respected writer, Mr. Kingsley Brown. This article deals with the conditions in connection with food so far as the militia camps are concerned.
I know, sir, that you do not like these things being read so I may have to follow the legal method of saying that I will adopt these words as my own, but I think at least a few paragraphs of this article might very well be read into the record. Here is what this writer says:
Down at Camp Niagara, where several thousand citizen-soldiers of the militia are taking their annual summer training, it was taking more than an orderly officer's bark to stem the flood of complaints we heard early this week about the food and the way it is served.
You know how the orderly officer goes around and inquires if there are any complaints and dares anybody to speak up. The article continues in this way:
Having spent several days living at camp Niagara we can say that the complaints were justified. Food was of a poor quality-we were served black potatoes that had obviously been frozen or diseased -the coffee-when it was available to those who turned up during the first hour of the mess period, was so cold it wasn't worth drinking If you did drink it, the effect was more emetic than stimulating.
Glassware and dishes weren't clean. They may have been dunked swiftly into water and then put out to dry, but they certainly weren't washed. Not those we sampled, at any rate.
The writer goes on in a very serious article and concludes in this way:
There is simply no excuse whatever for Canadian soldiers, at a home training camp in peacetime, being served in this fashion.
Canadian militiamen in training aren't looking for any fancy catering. They don't expect French chefs. They don't look for more than the normal camp mess furnishings.
But they have a right to expect good wholesome food, served up promptly in clean utensils. If the Canadian army is really interested in having its militiamen come back to camp next year, it will have to see that they get it.
That is an article which appeared in the Hamilton Spectator of July 12, 1956, written by Mr. Kingsley Brown. I agree with the rules which state that we should not quote
Supply-National Defence directly articles like this, but if there is no committee we must hammer and hammer away in order to get direct factual evidence in connection with conditions of this kind. I say that the opposition is left with no alternative but to bring forward the best evidence we can get.
This article by a respected writer is an indication of a condition which I think is no credit to the department. I submit it is something which demands an investigation and it certainly warrants a reply. As I said last night, I am pleased that this type of condition did not prevail overseas according to the reports we have, but apparently it does exist here. The important factor is that these men are part-time volunteers and many of them give these services at considerable inconvenience to themselves. If there is a real desire in the department to make use of the militia as a really active group within the defence set-up, then this type of condition should not exist. I ask that the minister consider some type of investigation so that there will be no necessity for articles of this sort appearing in our newspapers.

I think the committee to which the hon. member referred and the research program to which he referred are under the jurisdiction or guidance of my colleague, the Minister of Labour. If I may be permitted, I shall make a few observations about the other part of his speech, the part in which he referred to the remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich last night. We are, both as a government and as a department, very much concerned, of course, with the developments that are taking place today in the world, though it is probably too soon to evaluate them thoroughly. We have established our position, along with the other members of NATO, on the basis that the deterrent effect of our own capacity to reply in kind is the best defence we have and probably the best defence we can have. It is one thing for our possible opponents to launch an attack, either with thermonuclear weapons or without, as was indicated as a possibility by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, if they know there is no great defence against it or no great retaliatory capacity to meet it. If they do launch an attack, however, they know that they will get two for one or a very heavy counterattack. We must not forget that.
They are seeking now to shift the conflict into the commercial, economic and political fields, but I suggest that we should proceed very cautiously in accepting that. I also suggest that, as we have built our strength through NATO, we should consider any change in our attitude through NATO. Individually we may have different views to some extent within NATO, but I believe very strongly that the events of the past few years have amply demonstrated that we must keep NATO operating as one unit, whether it is in the field of defence or whether it is in the field of economics and associated activities. I think
Supply-National Defence that our strength will depend on the extent to which we are able to do that.
NATO is not static. It can change its emphasis and its approach if the facts warrant. I would conclude by saying: First, we should be very sure that the facts warrant any change; and, second, such change should be made only through NATO.

speechtext:
It was not my intention to enter the debate on the estimates of this particular department. My military experience is very limited. In fact, the only knowledge I have been able to glean in the matter was in my high school days when we took rifle drill with the old Lee Enfield rifles and were instructed in the niceties of bayonet warfare by a military sergeant-major whom most of us feared and some of us sincerely disliked. So I do not feel qualified to speak on this particular matter.
However, I should like to commend the minister for the expression of opinion to which we have just listened. Having listened to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich last night and to the hon. member for Mackenzie this morning, we appreciate of course their viewpoints, and we appreciate the splendid record of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich; but certainly I feel we ought to be very careful in the appraisal of the situation at the present time.
With regard to the suggestion that it may be time to withdraw troops from Germany, I realize that there may be something desirable in that, but certainly we ought to take a look at the other side of the picture. It may be true that the Soviet union is changing its strategy and moving into the field of economic and political warfare, but personally I am not convinced that they have given up the idea of military aggression and expansion. If they can divert our attention, get us to lower our guard and get us to neglect our defences, I should say that is exactly what they want us to do. Certainly if there is any suggestion that we let down on the military aspect of this proposition, I would say that we ought to approach that in a very cautious manner.
In an article in this morning's Globe and Mail, I believe, Chancellor Adenauer of West Germany expressed his views regarding the possibility of the withdrawal of the NATO forces from his country. He was very much perturbed over the situation. Certainly I should like to state again that, in any thought along this angle, this matter should certainly be studied very seriously lest we succumb to the temptation to take an easier route and thereby let down in our defence system.

speechtext:
I am sure that no one in this house is more qualified to speak on

Supply-National Defence this subject with which we dealt last evening than the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. Indeed, I am of those who believe that the statement he made last evening has been rather more loosely interpreted than the actual wording of his remarks based on his recent experience. Certainly there is no one in the house who will be misled by the smiles that have taken the place for the moment of the snarls of communism, but no one can lose sight of the fact that some change or detour has been made by the U.S.S.R. in recent times. The question of defence still remains pre-eminent, and as I understood the hon. member's remarks last evening in no way did he take a contrary view. Nevertheless he did suggest that in the change that has taken place in the U.S.S.R. there is a challenge to free enterprise and private enterprise everywhere in the world on the part of the U.S.S.R. in its new trade policy.
In order that the people of this country will not be misled by communism our newspapers make a commanding and important contribution to the building of public sentiment. I should have liked to hear the hon. member for Mackenzie comment on the reported speech of Mr. William Irvine, a former member of this house, who, if reported correctly, made an irresponsible speech, a speech dangerous because of its nature, a speech in which in fulsome words he warmly commended the U.S.S.R. for its high grade democracy. I hope we shall have a copy of that speech, for it is one of those things that will be used by the U.S.S.R. as a propaganda means to indicate how wonderful things are under communism, however divergent that view may be from the actual facts.
Sir, I rise for the purpose of paying a particular tribute to the foreign language press of this country. Other than the 15 or so communist papers that are published, the remainder of the 140 foreign language papers are making a wonderful contribution in their stand against communism and also in meeting the kind of propaganda to which I have just made reference. I should like to ask the minister this question. What was the total amount expended last year on advertising by the Department of National Defence? I have a question on the order paper in that regard and I should like the minister to give me an answer thereto. It is question No. 551.
I believe that the non-English and nonFrench press of this country, other than the communist press, deserves a fair and more reasonable share of the national advertising than it has been receiving in the past. The


foreign language press has a reading public among the peoples of the various languages represented by that press and it deserves at least a reasonable and fair share of the national advertising done by the government of Canada. I do not mean lay way of a subsidy or honorarium, but it would give that press the means of continuing the work it is doing to meet the infiltration among foreign language groups in which communism is continually engaged.
I should like the minister to say first of all what was the total amount spent by his department on national advertising, recruiting advertising, during the last year, or in the last two years if he has the information, and how much has been paid to the foreign language press. Personally I feel that the foreign language press, the non-communist group, and I re-emphasize that, is doing a great and valuable service to Canada and also for the preservation of the democratic way of life. Relieving that, I feel that every consideration should be given not only by the Department of National Defence but by other departments of the government to preserving this press in the work it is doing, not by handouts or by assistance but simply by the allocation of a reasonable and fair share of national advertising.

then go ahead and prepare the meals from them. If my information is correct, in some cases at least they receive a per diem allowance and then feed the men out of that. I think it is under those circumstances particularly that complaints and difficulties arise as far as messing at militia camps is concerned. In any event, it seems to me that where there have been complaints and difficulties with respect to feeding of men at militia camps the caterers who have been in charge where these complaints arise should not be re-employed.
I do not know upon what basis these contracts are entered into. I do not know whether or not the contract is given to them for the whole course of the camp and, no matter what kind of food they put out, they continue to have the messing contract. But if that is the case, it should be issued on the basis that if the food is not satisfactory they are finished and somebody else goes in. I wonder whether the minister can just tell us what the provisions are in that regard. As has been indicated by other members, in order to attract members of the militia to these camps, it is absolutely essential that the best possible meals that can be prepared and given to the men under camp conditions should be provided. These people are taking their holidays when they are at these camps. Certain it is that if they are not reasonably well fed they are not going to come back the next year.

speechtext: I may say that I agree entirely with the hon. member for Calgary North. Since the chairman, I think very wisely, has allowed us to revert to discussion of a former matter, and since the question of what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said last night has been given some consideration and perhaps has had placed upon it an interpretation which he had no intention of having placed upon it, I think it is only fitting that I draw to the attention of the house and of the people throughout the country this important statement which appeared on September 19, 1955. As others have already said, I think the great danger is that we shall begin to "take things too easy".
This is a statement by Nikita S. Khrushchev, secretary of the communist party in Russia, as reported in the New York Herald Tribune of September 19, 1955. I am quoting from a book entitled "An Idea to Win the World" by Peter Howard.	The only
authority I have is this book but I am quite confident that the book is correct. Here are the words:
Russia's smiles are sincere, but this doesn't change our conviction that Communism will triumph throughout the world.
We will win, but we will not have to go to war about it.
We told Dr. Adenauer very frankly that Western Germany was going the way of capitalist decay. The way of the future is the way of the German Democratic Republic (Communist East Germany). Eventually all Germany will see the right way.
They say in the West that something has changed since the Geneva conference. They say that the Soviet leaders smile, but that their actions do not match their smiles. But the smiles are sincere. They are not artificial. We wish to live in peace. But if anyone thinks that our smiles mean that we abandon the teachings of Marx and Lenin or abandon our Communist road, then they are fooling themselves. You might as well say that Easter always falls on Tuesday.
We are for co-existence. But we are also for the growth of Communism. The only reason we are for co-existence is that in actual fact we are confronted with the reality of two different systems. You capitalists go your way so long as you do not see that it is the way of the blind.
Victory for Socialism? We don't have to go to war to obtain this victory. Peaceful competition will be enough. We will see who is right. If you really think (addressing the capitalist world) that your system is not too old and rotten, if you believe that it is really possible to keep in
6234	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the race, go ahead and try and compete. But the truth is on the side of our people. Our people do not depend on your love or your hate.
Now I should like to draw a matter to the attention of the people throughout the country and of those in the house who have not had this fact impressed upon them. If Khrushchev were speaking as a Russian in that speech and if he represented Russia, we might say, "Well, the Russian people will probably change their minds". But Khrushchev is not speaking as a Russian. He is speaking as a member of the communist conspiracy. There are not more than seven million or eight million of these people in Russia, I am told. However, they dominate the whole of Russia with its 200 million people, they dominate China and they will dominate every area that will come under their control.
Who are these people? They are peoples whose minds will not change. They are people who are not of our race. They are alien people. Someone asked me yesterday if I could give an idea of who they are. May I say that two years ago I clearly implied who they are. They are Turko-Mongo-lian Reds. There will be those who will laugh, but the laugh will be on the other side of their faces when they get a little bit more knowledge. So many people, because they do not happen to know the facts, assume that nobody else knows them. In all our dealings in Canada as a whole and in this house, let us just bear in mind the fact that we are not dealing with a people whose blood to any extent resembles ours at all but that we are dealing with a group of alien people who are definitely aiming to rule the world.

I see the hon. member for Prince Albert in his seat. I have some remarks that may affect him, and I want to make them while he is still in the house. 
I think it was a great privilege for those of us who were on the trip last year overseas to the NATO parliamentary conference to be able to go on afterwards to our troops in Germany and particularly to visit our air division in southern France and southern Germany. I confess that just about this time last year I played hookey and neglected my duties here for about three weeks before that conference to travel in different parts of Europe, and I was very fortunate to be in western Europe at the time of the biggest sham battle, as we used to call them when I was younger, in the history of the world. That is the one that they call "Carte Blanche", in which the whole action was fought under as nearly realistic warlike conditions as it was possible to make them. It began with a simulated attack from east of the iron curtain, and the minute it began everything went into action right across the continent of Europe from Norway to the Mediterranean and the Black sea. The fighting was all carried out under service conditions.
As the hon. members for Calgary North and Prince Albert will remember, when we were privileged to visit our forces in Germany and southern France we had the great privilege of being briefed by the commanders of our first Canadian air division. I also had the great privilege of taking a good deal of time off and studying the actual reports of this carte blanche manoeuvre, and I think it was one of the most instructive things of modern times. I shall not trespass on the good will of the house today except to say that, from the official reports published, if it had been a real war and not just a pretending war, at the end of 48 hours no military formation of any kind by land, sea and air would have been able to carry on as an organized military entity.
But the part that particularly impressed me, as a Canadian M.P. visiting our first Canadian air division, apart from the natural attraction of having that wonderful visit with those very wonderful men, was to find the actual results of what took place in that carte blanche exercise. The actual statistics show that, whereas the Canadian air division competed with all other allied air divisions on a basis of equality, man for man and plane for plane our R.C.A.F. men and our R.C.A.F. units did 20 per cent better than any other NATO unit. When we asked the commanders and the staff officers responsible for that really wonderful performance what the reason was, they said with characteristic modesty that they thought that the Canadian was just as good as anybody else fighting on either side of that pretended battle line but they thought that the Canadian planes were a little better because they had found that

Supply-National Defence question of whether or not we ought to dispose of surplus aircraft to the state of Israel.
I must confess that, this morning and on recent days when the hon. member for Prince Albert rose and in tones of righteous indignation put the government on the spot for not more quickly making up its mind whether or not to sell these aircraft to Israel, I could hardly believe my own ears. I remember very well on January 31 when that very same gentleman, the hon. member for Prince Albert, in tones of even more fervent and righteous indignation moved the following resolution, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition:
In view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries in that area not within the NATO alliance: and also condemns the government for the lack of candour with which the matter has been dealt with in this house.

I have seen some very good generals in action, including the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, who knew how to throw up a good smokescreen when he had to retreat, but I have never seen a cleverer smokescreen thrown up than by the hon. member for Prince Albert in trying to disguise the back somersault that the Conservative party is trying to accomplish with this business of aircraft for Israel.
I will say that my hon. friend from Vancouver East cannot in any way be criticized for this, because we all know he was absent from the house when this matter was discussed. I have been looking up the names of the people who voted for this absolute embargo on the selling of any planes to Israel, and among others who voted for that is the same gentleman who is now rising and in stentorian tones criticizing the government for being so slow. Aitken (Miss), Argue, Barnett, Bell, Bennett (Miss), Blair, Brooks, Bryce, Bryson, Cameron (Nanaimo), Cardiff, Castleden, Charlton, Churchill, Coldwell, Diefenbaker.

I happen to know a little about this remarkable conversion of the hon. member for Prince Albert. It so happened that by accident he made his speech one day before I got there. So, when I got to Edmonton on my way back to Ottawa from Vancouver, what did I read? I read that the same hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Prince Albert, who had moved this very resolution in the house for an absolute embargo on the shipment of war planes to Israel, had, like Saul on the road to Damascus, been stricken by a great light when he got to Edmonton. When he got there he said that it might be a good idea if we supplied all sorts of planes to Israel so that they could have the means to defend themselves.

In reply to the hon. member for York-Scarborough I would say that as far as the heavy four-engine planes are concerned we have no operational planes in that category except, of course, in transport command and in maritime reconnaissance command. We do train and develop pilots to supply our needs in those two commands. I would also point out that we are part of a whole set-up comprising NATO in which each nation has its own particular part to play and we are not called upon to provide either strategic bombers or bomber fleets of four engine planes. is in the fighter field, other than the two commands I have mentioned. Therefore we have no bomber command pilot training unit or the nucleus of one.

It would just be too expensive a luxury.
I think it is better that we conform to the NATO idea and try to achieve the very best results we can in the fields where we are expected to operate. The last thing I would say regarding heavy bombers is that we do not, of course, have any thermonuclear weapons in this country, and that is the type of weapon for which the modern, heavy, four-engine bombers are designed.

speechtext:

This board since its formation in 1940 has contributed greatly to the solution of military problems affecting both Canada and the United States and has built up an excellent record of achievement through the years. It is a purely advisory board, not concerned with policy but only with working out joint arrangements once policy has been settled by the governments concerned.
When that board was set up in 1940, my understanding was that its primary function was to make recommendations on policy. But according to the minister's statement, at the present time the board has absolutely nothing to do with policy or with recommending policy but merely helps to work out the details of policy once that policy has been decided by some other authority. Is that correct?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I presume the board can make recommendations to the government if it chooses to do so. However, it cannot decide any matter. It can make recommendations to the governments concerned. But usually most of its work consists of taking projects or developments that have been agreed upon and working out the mechanics as between the two countries, as to how the work will be done, and generally taking such steps as are necessary to put an agreed plan into effect.

Supply-National Defence

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Why could that not be done a good deal more effectively by the defence department itself, or by the officials of the defence department aided, if necessary, by officials of the external affairs department and of the Department of Defence Production? Once policy has been decided, why is it necessary to drag in this outside board to help carry out the details?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It is a joint board of the two countries, and they are not dragged in at all. They are given a very appreciable amount Of work to do. The agenda of this board is always quite heavy. The board meets for several days at each meeting. The fact is that it is a joint board-I have given only the names of the Canadian section, and there is a corresponding United States section-and it is more or less a clearing house. A great deal of work must be cleared through the Department of External Affairs by the board; and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and some services are sometimes involved in the matters in hand and others are not. The board can work with the service in each country that is involved.
I think probably the best commentary I could make is that the board has now been jn existence for something like 16 years-15 anyway-and it has proved its usefulness. It has proved especially that it had great usefulness in the period of the cold war. It affords a very ready and available instrument to carry into effect joint decisions by the two countries, to take cognizance of the problems involved and to formulate methods of meeting those problems.
In practice, just as a matter of fact I can say that in my time, which has not been too Jong, it has proved to be very helpful and very useful and a very ready means of getting things done. Otherwise each problem might involve a different group of people and you would have numerous committees all over the place. This board is in the nature of a clearing house to deal with decisions which have been taken.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Why should the chairman not be a member of the minister's own department. I ask that question because quite a serious charge was made on this question, as the minister knows, by General Simonds. The general had this to say:
.. The existence of the permanent joint board on defence adds further confusion to the direction of our military affairs. This organization came into being during the period of world war II when Canada was a belligerent and the United States was still neutral, and at that time was a useful instrument for obtaining some co-ordination of measures for North American defence. Now it simply acts as a barrier to closer liaison between the Canadian and U.S. chiefs of staff, and is redundant in so far as its military activities are concerned.
IMr. Campney.]
Then he went on to say:
But the chairman has a more ready access to senior cabinet ministers than have the chiefs of staff. Whatever the terms of reference may be, many of the expressed views of ministers bear the unmistakable imprint of the influence of an intellect more remarkable for its bias toward pseudoscience and gadgetry, than for its record of sound military judgment.
Why is it that the chairman of the Canadian section of this joint permanent defence board is not an official of the Department of National Defence? It would seem that by making an arrangement of that type the weaknesses claimed by General Simonds would be removed.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Well, I do not know why a member of the Department of National Defence was not made chairman. I was not involved in administrative proceedings at that time. I can make only two observations. One is that having worked with the board for two years, I would not have thought of having a chairman from my department for the reason that the board deals with so many departments and has so many responsibilities and detailed activities that are not completely within the purview of my department. It seems to me that the founding fathers who set up this board did a very proper thing when they picked an independent chairman. The same thing has applied in the United States. Their section of the board is built the same as ours and the chiefs of staff have their representatives on the board the same as ours. I think when the first board was instituted Mayor LaGuardia of New York was appointed by the President of the United States to head their section.
I cannot agree with the comment the hon. gentleman has made. My experience only covers two years, but I have seen no indication of any of the circumstances he has outlined in my relations with the board. I have heard no criticism of the board before this from anyone, including other chiefs of staff who were on the board. Therefore I just have to take my own point of view, which is that I think the board is useful. It does excellent work and it fills a real need. In my experience it has not, as far as I know, slowed up any consideration of matters as between the two countries. On the contrary, it has expedited matters. Nor has it interfered with the existing rights of the chiefs of staff of the two countries concerned. The chiefs of staff here and the chiefs of staff of the United States can go back and forth and converse or meet with their opposite numbers at will. That goes on all the time. There is no let or hindrance about it that I know of.
This board deals with a wider field, including some defence matters in which they

are interested. The reason that the three vice chiefs of staff are there representing their chiefs in each nation is to have continuity and a continual appreciation on the part of both countries of all the problems that are being worked out by the board. As I say, I have found the board very helpful and very useful, and I have not seen any necessity to criticize it nor, so far as I know, has anybody else except General Simonds. Probably that is quite all right, because in all these things we have critics and supporters and so on, but I have not had any criticism at all conveyed to me.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS

My final subject is a matter of administration of the air force. Apparently provision is made for the payment of a gratuity under certain conditions to officers who have served in the air force, but there is the restriction that if they are discharged or released on medical grounds, then they
Supply-National Defence do not get the full amount of the gratuity. They have deducted from that whatever is taken out of the regular pay for pension, what is called deferred pay. Thus if a man's gratuity amounts to $1,500 and he has deferred pay accumulated, which of course is being accumulated to go toward his pension when he retires, if he drops out for medical reasons he does not get the full $1,500 but only $1,500 less the amount of his own deferred pay. That is done, I am told, under Q.R. (air) article 206.23 (6) (a). It seems to me unfair that he should not get the full gratuity as well as the amount that has been deducted to apply to his future pension. Can the minister have that situation checked?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: I understand the situation is that when a man enrols for a short-service commission he contracts to serve for a certain period of time, which I think is five years. If he completes his service in accordance with the contract he gets his gratuity. If during that time he is pensionable and becomes ill by reason of his service, he receives a pension. If he does not complete his term he receives only the amount he has paid in himself toward a gratuity but not the portion that would be put up by the government. In other words, he has failed to complete his contract and while he does not lose by that so far as his own contributions are concerned, because he gets those back, he does not get the added sum that would be put up by the government to complete his gratuity.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: But if he suffers a disability as the result of a flying accident why should-

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then he is pensioned.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Pardon?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: If he suffers a disability by reason of an accident within the scope of his employment he receives a pension.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: He would receive a disability pension?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: But why should that have anything to do with his gratuity? Why should that reduce his gratuity? We have always understood that a disability pension is intended to bring the man who has suffered a disability up to an even starting point with the man who has not been disabled.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
That is true, but the pension compensates for the fact that he has not been able to complete his contract because of what has happened. The fact is that it more than compensates him for the fact he has not completed his contract, and therefore he gets

Supply-National Defence back what he has put in but he does not get the additional gratuity.
I suppose we should look at the picture as a whole. He is paid his pension because he has not completed his contract for a valid reason, in this case an accident. The matter is fairly administered, as I see it. He cannot have the full gratuity unless he has completed his full contract, but he can always get back what he has paid in. If the hon. member has a specific case he would like me to look into I should be glad to do so, but I have stated the general rule as I understand it.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS

I wonder if the minister would look into the situation further because I am afraid there is an unfairness, in that the disability pension is being linked up with the gratuity and I do not think that should be taken into consideration in arriving at the gratuity.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: I will be glad to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would give us a number of details showing the breakdown of responsibility as between his department and the Department of Defence Production in obtaining supplies and equipment for use particularly by the air force, because my subsequent observations will apply to that. The type of material I have in mind is piping, tubing, and all the other mechanical purchases which are made for supply purposes.
We know that the Department of Defence Production acts as purchasing agent for the minister's department in that respect, but I would like to know who has the responsibility for such things as auditing these parts and making sure that the material delivered is the same as that which has been requisitioned. Who has the responsibility for describing the material required and making sure it is the proper material and that it is given the proper coding? Who has the responsibility for ascertaining the quantities required, the point at which orders should be given and that type of thing?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a subject on which I would not attempt to go into any great detail, but generally speaking


we as the Department of National Defence, subject to some small exceptions, are not permitted to purchase for our requirements. If the purchasing involves land for the construction of airports our agent is the Department of Transport. If the purchase is for commodities or construction or to meet other needs we have we make a requisition on the Department of Defence Production for what we want. The specifications for what we want are our responsibility. We have to lay down specifically and carefully the type of thing we want. We then send that with a requisition to the Department of Defence Production and they take such steps as they deem advisable-usually by tender or on a contract basis-to procure the thing we want at a proper price. That is their responsibility.
If it is something that has to be manufactured or built, our inspection staff follows the matter along until it is ready for delivery. We are responsible for having received everything we ask for because we have planned or specified it and have inspected it. We follow the process along and have to take the responsibility of seeing that we obtain what we have ordered and then we pay for it. That is a very simple outline but 1 think it is essentially a correct one.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, how about my final question regarding the point at which it is decided to reorder, the quantities that are ordered and the quantities required? Is that a decision of the Department of National Defence or the Department of Defence Production?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: If I understood the hon. member correctly I think under the circumstances he mentioned it would be a service decision. In other words, if we said we wanted X number of something and could only get Y, we would have to decide whether we would take none or all. In other words the Department of Defence Production is our agent, and in matters of the kind just mentioned it would be our decision.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The
minister in his reply has not mentioned any audit or check on this purchasing procedure, but he has specifically accepted the responsibility of his own department for stating the specifications of commodities required, for establishing the quantities required and determining the point at which the order is to be placed; that is, when the stock is low enough to require an order.
In order to be helpful to the minister I would like to give him a few contracts that he might look at to see just how well his current procedures are working out. The difficulty here, I might say, is in some re-

spects that of assessing the responsibility as to where certain errors occur. If the minister will go back and look at a particular requisition which ended up as tender B-18/28/16, he will find included in that a requirement for a part which showed on the contract as No. H-2320-30. That was a bolt. The original order placed by the Department of Defence Production was for 1,995 at a cost of approximately $16 each. The interesting thing about this is that if that part had been properly quoted as VS-2320-30 it would have indicated that it was manufactured by a company in California, and that company retails this bolt at $2.02. As far as I know it could have been brought into Canada duty free.
The main point is that here is a case where the department appears to have paid several times what they should have paid for the same article. There was a slip-up somewhere in the ordering system, and I would assume also in the specifications sent out by the department.
Again on the same contract there is another item designated 2319-27, also a bolt. Again the initials "VS" were left off and the result was that this article was purchased in Canada at approximately $4 each rather than from the company which manufactures and sells it retail at 82 cents. I want to point out that in these particular instances the article had been imported into Canada by an intermediary and there was no question of placing an order in Canada as against placing it in the United States.
Another thing which should be watched more carefully is the checking of merchandise against specifications. There were certain specifications that called for new material, but in these cases which I shall mention I think the minister will find that surplus material was supplied while new material prices were charged. The contract numbers include B18-28-NA2; B18-28-NS1 and B18-28-NA1. I give the minister these numbers so he can follow up this matter if he is sincerely interested. It was suggested by the person who is conversant with this situation that if this material had been carefully inspected it would not have been accepted.
I have a few other cases here having to do with quantities. I have referred to numbers being left off in the specifications; I have referred to the need of checking material when it is received, and I should like to deal now with quantities. One contract demand I have in mind is No. 511,301, which became contract B18-38-196. This contract was given out back in 1953 and the department ordered
5,000	pieces of AN839-16, which was an 67509-397
Supply-National Defence elbow tube to tube. According to the latest information I have the great majority of these items are still in stock and they cost $25,000 three years ago. It has been suggested that this material actually was not required.
I have various bits of information of this type but I am not going to spend undue time exploring every last item. However, I think it shows two things; first, the need for the minister to investigate carefully his relations with the Department of Defence Production and the information he is supplying; and second, the need for a much more adequate audit system on parts and supplies than that which exists at the present time. All the items I have referred to have to do with the air force, which is why I have brought up the matter at this time.
It seems to me that various parts of the minister's department are not operating in the most efficient manner. There would appear to be a definite tendency to order unduly large quantities of many items in a haphazard fashion without any relation to previous use and consumption or to proposed use and consumption. There is as far as I can see, and the minister has given no indication today, no attempt to audit these items. The Department of Defence Production operate simply as a purchasing agent, and I gather they will purchase anything asked for by the minister. That department makes no attempt to check, so therefore the responsibility must lie with the minister. The ordering practices and the contract demands which have been met I believe represent many hundreds of thousands if not many millions of dollars worth of material which is simply being left in stock with no sign of immediate usage.

speechtext: There is one other matter which has rather surprised me in these estimates with regard to the civilian personnel. I also wonder what the duties of these messmen are that require such a large number. As a matter of fact there would appear to be almost one messman for every 20 people in the R.C.A.F.

speechtext:
I understand that the increase arises from the restriction of hours at radar stations and the 24-hour operation of those stations. It has been necessary to augment staff in various cases. In addition, there have been a very substantial number of additional facilities opened during the past year.
As to what constitutes the duties of a messman, I should think they would be persons who do almost anything pertaining to the housekeeping for the mess, the kitchen work, the cleaning up and so on. I cannot authoritatively say just what the scope of their activities is, but as a matter of fact I

should think the increase of 21 must mean that in the over-all picture there have been also some reductions. subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
My question was not so
much with regard to the small addition of 21 but as to why there were approximately 2,000 of them in any event. Why are so many messmen needed in the R.C.A.F., considerably more than twice as many, nearly two and a half times as many, as for the army with the same type of personnel?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: For one thing I think it is probably attributable to the fact that we have a very great number of small units in the air force, more than we have in the regular army. I am not sure whether the term "messmen" means the same thing in both services or whether in the air force it embraces other duties. I do not know that, but it is apparent that the air force has many more small units where messmen are required, and I am sure that would add to the total number.

Whilst the difference in
the number of units might explain some of this difference, I do not think it would by any means explain all of it. There are numbers of small units in the army as well as in the air force. I think the total number of units in the army, according to the list the minister gave, was 500 odd. Some of those must be very small units. It seems to me there is far too great a disparity. It is a matter the minister perhaps should look into. It looks like poor administration somehow.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS

speechtext:
I shall only take a few minutes, and it is more to get myself oriented for the debate that may come later in connection with defence pro-dution. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace asked what type of liaison there was between the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production. I am thinking of probably something much wider in policy than the items he was mentioning, in connection with the over-all procurement of aircraft and the natural worries that we have in keeping our aircraft plants in production.
Has the minister, along with the Minister of Defence Production and perhaps the Minister of Transport, considered at all the

advisability of sponsoring the production in Canada of a military transport plane? I have spoken about this in previous years, and I have indicated that all planes of this type in other countries have first of all been of military origin and then carried on as a civil type transport. It appears to be of vital necessity, if we are not going to have our aircraft plants in a boom or bust cycle, that we have some continuity in production. Now I shall tie the question right down to the remarks that were made by the minister in connection with the emphasis that he thought might be placed in the future on the carriage of airborne troops, as distinct from the paratroops on whom the emphasis has been heretofore. These were his words at page 5212 of Hansard:
For example, if aircraft such as the C-119 were used, apart altogether from the cost of ground facilities and air crew, but allowing for reserve aircraft, it would require 148 planes, at a cost of about $150 million, to provide a one-up lift for an army brigade without its heavy equipment.
Have there been any discussions between the minister and the Minister of Defence Production and perhaps the Minister of Transport as well as to the feasibility of using a requirement such as this to create a very strong and adequate civil reserve of aircraft?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: The answer is no. In our department we are studying for our own purposes the question of the provision of transport, but to my knowledge there has not been any conference of the nature mentioned by the hon. member.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It seems to me that the least that should be done is to study the plan used in the United States. As I say, much civil transport has resulted there from the original production of a military type plane and the fact, as I understand it, that the civil aircraft authorities and the government have made leasing arrangements with civilian operators under which the planes that have been produced are being operated by the regular cargo carriers and are on a 48-hour recall basis. It is particularly noteworthy that they are on a recall basis with crews supplied. It seems to me that the minister is maybe hesitant here about $150 million to produce 148 transport planes, but at the same time he has indicated that we have spent $120 million odd on the pre-production costs for the CF-100. That is a plane which is very necessary but has no place in civilian use.
I am not going to blame the minister. I think perhaps some sort of liaison is required, and that possibly two or three of the gentlemen on the treasury benches should be called to a meeting. It probably would be called 67509-397J
Supply-National Defence by the Minister of Defence Production. I do believe that some serious thought should be given to this problem. I will only say, and I may have to repeat it tonight, that if such a plan is not put into effect we will have a constant repetition of what I have termed the boom and bust in aircraft production.
If we are having stretch-outs, as we are now, then I assume we can possibly say there is nothing to fill in to keep the production line going, to keep the engineers on the job and stay abreast of technical developments. If that is not the case, then possibly we have been slow in the development of the replacement aircraft, the CF-105, and I do not believe that because I think it has come along as fast as it could come along anywhere. Frankly, I think we may be a little optimistic when we talk about two or three years. It may be longer than that, but even at that it is keeping pace with developments in other countries.
If these two reasons are not the reasons for the stretch-out, and I think the first one can be corrected, then I can only assume that the minister cannot recruit enough pilots to put in his machines, that he can build them faster than he can get men to fly them. Last year I asked for a return along this line. I have not the figures before me, but I think we had something like 5,000 applicants for aircrew enlistment. Somewhere along the line we dropped 4,000 of them, whether by reason of physical disability or inability to meet flying standards after training had commenced. We ended up with about 1,000, and as I recall it that number was only enough to meet the replacement program.
If the two other reasons are not the real reasons here, and I think one of them can be corrected, then we should take a very serious look at the manpower question. The matter of personnel for aircrew in the air force may be only part of the problem. It may be that we have to look farther afield than that and assess manpower requirements in all branches of industry and the forces. But something should be done. Whether through liaison among those on the treasury benches or liaison as to the methods used to establish a regular production line in other countries, action is required in either case.

Periodically complaints come in with regard to too many aircraft flying low over built-up areas. Periodically complaints are lodged and there is an abate-

Supply-National Defence ment of the noise and trouble, and then periodically it recurs. Just now in St. James and Winnipeg complaints are being made with regard to low flying aircraft.

There is an element of danger there and if the flyers are student flyers people naturally get nervous. The noise is a troublesome thing.
I should like to compliment the night flyers on the success with which they complete their circuit with regularity and the accuracy with which they keep on course, because they go right over my house from eleven o'clock at night to 12.30 or from 11.30 to one o'clock. I would not object to it in Ottawa but my habits at home are much more regular and I find it a bit annoying. I appreciate the complaints raised by other citizens of St. James and Winnipeg with regard to low flying aircraft, particularly at night. What is the situation so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS

speechtext: I might mention that this came to my attention through articles in the Winnipeg Tribune of July 9 and the Winnipeg Free Press of July 4, indicating that the matter had been taken up with the city council. I presume that complaints will be registered with the authorities.

{Mr. Churchill.]

We all realize that on certain occasions there may be an urgent necessity for that procedure, but I think we should realize also that the department are flouting these regulations in the instructions they are issuing to their pilots.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PORTFOLIOS OF POST OFFICE AND VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Extensive reorganization is taking place in our air force auxiliary and reserve programs this year, according to the information supplied by the minister in the white paper. As has been typical of the activities in our air force reserve, I find it somewhat difficult to understand the logic in all the changes that are taking place. During

the past ten years in Canada, since the end of world war II, the air force reserve has had a rather chequered career and from time to time in this house we have had statements of a somewhat contradictory nature.
For example, as I have said before, at one time we were told that the reserve was the backbone of our defence program in this country and that eventually they would be supplied with CF-100 all-weather fighters. We raised some objection as to the feasibility of that scheme because of the nature of the training difficulties, and we recommended that the personnel might be more suitably employed on a less complex aircraft from a navigational standpoint, namely the F-86. In 1954 the then minister of national defence, in reply to suggestions of that kind, as reported at page 4991 of Hansard, of May 21, 1954 said this:
There is another reason, and that is that these Sabre fighters are really not well suited for the air defence of Canada. They have a relatively short range, they have only one pilot; they have not a complete set of navigational instruments, and if they went into the air and got into a dogfight in Canada they might have great difficulty in getting back to their airfield.
Notwithstanding that statement of two years ago we have received the information that six, I think it is, of our reserve squadrons are going to be equipped with F-86 Sabres for the defence of Canada. I would agree that this is a good move, as we suggested some two or three years ago, but certain aspects of the reorganization are difficult to understand. In the white paper, in reference to the Canadian army, the minister says there is to be emphasis on the air portability of our army. If that is to be the emphasis so far as the army is concerned, it would seem to me that the demand for reserve flying personnel will be larger than it has ever been hitherto.
That consideration gives rise to the querying of the disbanding of a fully operational squadron such as the 424 Hamilton squadron. I should like to ask the minister how it is anticipated that we are going to move toward the objective of air portability and mobility of the army if we continue to disband reserve air crew who are fully operational.
In the white paper there is also some reference to the necessity for developing a mobile striking force-and I think these are the words used-which would be able to deal rapidly with any enemy lodgments in Canada. It seems to me that here again is a function that could be adequately carried out by air force reserve people. The de Havilland Otter which is being used extensively by the United States air force for air portability purposes is capable of carrying 10 fully equipped
Industrial Relations
combat troops and, in cases of airborne operations as contrasted with air portable operations, it is possible to carry out paratroop dropping at speeds of between 60 miles per hour and 140 miles per hour. To summarize this point, in the face of these growing needs particularly in connection with air transport responsibilities, I find it difficult to understand the action on the part of the Department of National Defence in disbanding fully qualified air crew and fully operational reserve squadrons.
I might also refer to the possible use of reserve people in carrying out international army exercises. Some comment has been made today concerning the necessity for maintaining large numbers of Canadian troops in Europe. In this day of rapid air transportation there is no reason why we could not make the army reserve more attractive by carrying out international exercises by means of an enlarged R.C.A.F. transport command. The further difficulty was raised last evening as to how our personnel already in Europe might be evacuated in the event of necessity.
