subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 441, to provide for pay for statutory holidays for employees and for pay for work performed on statutory holidays.	.

Industrial Relations
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when this bill was introduced and given first reading last Monday, it is a companion to Bill No. 211 which was under debate at the second reading stage on May 11 of this year. I believe that in the case of both of these bills, this is the first time their subject matter has been presented to the federal parliament in the form of actual bills. The proposals contained in these two bills have frequently been presented to parliament, but as I have already indicated, I believe for the first time they are before parliament in legislative form.
As hon. members will recall, the purpose of the other bill, Bill No. 211, is to make provision for at least two weeks' annual vacation with pay for all workers in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. The purpose of this companion bill, Bill No. 441, is to make a parallel provision for these same workers, namely the provision of at least eight statutory holidays each year with pay.
Perhaps I might indicate at this point the actual holidays suggested in this bill. They are: New Year's day, Good Friday, Victoria day, Dominion day, Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day. I would point out that these are holidays which are observed to a greater or lesser extent in all parts of Canada. There are, perhaps, other holidays which are celebrated in different parts of Canada. For example, in the western provinces, here in Ontario and in some other areas there is observed in August what is known in urban areas at any rate as civic holiday, and in the province of Quebec there are holidays like St. Jean Baptiste day, and others. That is indeed the reason that this bill provides for a minimum of eight statutory holidays; for it is part of my thinking that there are other liolidays in different areas which could be covered by provincial legislation.
To say a further word as to what is actually provided in this bill, may I point out that it requires that every employee under federal labour jurisdiction who is permitted-by virtue of working conditions or on any other basis-to be off work on the eight statutory holidays shall receive his regular pay in full for each of those eight statutory holidays. The bill also provides that if anyone is required to work on any of those statutory holidays-this is a recognition of the fact that there are certain services that have to be performed every day the year round, and therefore some people will have to work on gome of those days-he shall receive his regular pay plus overtime pay for the work he does, at what is known as double time.

Another provision, Mr. Speaker, is that nothing in the bill shall affect any provision, so far as statutory holidays with pay are concerned, in any legislation, contract of employment, or custom that is better than is set out in this bill. In other words, salaried employees or persons in a managerial capacity who already have, by arrangement or by custom or by contract, statutory holidays without any loss of pay, do not suffer any loss of whatever provision they now have by virtue of this bill, and that is spelled out in one of the clauses. On the other hand, the bill also has a clear-cut provision that its minimum requirement shall supersede any provision that is less favourable to employees than those set out in this bill.
There are various other detailed provisions worked out in Bill No. 441. I will not take the time of the house to go into them now, for they are the kind of details that could be discussed either in committee of the whole on the bill or in the industrial relations committee, to which I would hope that this bill might be referred for study after second reading. However, I invite hon. members to study the detailed provisions of Bill No. 441, as indeed I invited them to study the details of Bill No. 211, so they will realize that there is before them not just a general or pious resolution but a concrete piece of legislative machinery to make possible the immediate putting into effect of the principle of statutory holidays with pay for all employees who come under the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament.
As hon. members realize, it is not a great period of time since for the average industrial worker there was no such thing as pay for any day on which he did not work, either in terms of an annual vacation or in terms of a statutory holiday. None of us, in taking part in debates in this house, like to be at all personal, but I am sure my experience is like that of many other members here, namely that I can think of persons whom I have known who were industrial workers, persons close indeed to me, who through the whole of their lives never knew what it was to have a vacation with pay or to get paid for statutory holidays on which they did not work.
It is good to know that we are moving on and that slowly but surely the pattern is changing. In the old days industrial workers got time off, all right; they got statutory holidays because the shop was shut down, but there was no pay for them for those days. They also had vacations, but either they took them at a loss of pay or they were because of unemployment, and one would not exactly call such periods vacations.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, we have moved on and the pattern is beginning to take shape,

namely that industrial workers-indeed, all workers in a community such as ours-should as a matter of right have both the vacations with pay covered in the other bill and the statutory holidays with pay provided in this bill, second reading of which I am now presenting to the house.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, for a considerable period of time there was something of a division which I think was not good for our society, in that salaried people seemed to get statutory holidays without any loss of pay. In other words, people who were on monthly or annual salary did not suffer because certain days were declared to be public or statutory holidays. On the other hand wage earners, industrial workers and those on hourly rates of pay have had quite a struggle trying to achieve recognition of the fact that they, too, should be paid their regular pay for statutory holidays.
I remind hon. members that the request for legislation to provide these two items-annual vacations with pay, at least two weeks in that case, and also at least eight statutory holidays with pay-is part of the program of the new Canadian Labour Congress. As a matter of fact the new Canadian Labour Congress in that respect is simply carrying forward what were the requests of the constituent organizations which came together to make up that congress. It seems to me we now have a chance in this House of Commons to recognize this new era in Canadian labour history, an era marked by the birth of the Canadian Labour Congress, by dealing favourably with this bill and with the other one which taken together lay before parliament a major item of policy in the platform of the new congress.
I hope hon. members will give serious consideration to the representations that have been made in this connection by organized labour, and that they will recognize that it is hardly fair, in view of the fact that we as a parliament are responsible for some of the statutory holidays being observed-for example, Victoria day and Dominion day as well as some others, are holidays by virtue of federal statutes-for us to require that these holidays be observed and not take cognizance of the fact that the result is that some people in the observance of those holidays do not lose their pay and others do. Surely the way to get around that unfairness is to pass what might be called ancillary legislation such as is contained in these two bills and make it clear that the holidays which we require to be observed-indeed, all of them as set out in this bill-shall be days when all those who contribute to the economy of this country, whether they be salaried
Industrial Relations
workers or wage earners on hourly rates of pay, shall have those holidays without loss of pay.
Mr. Speaker, it has been an argument I have used with respect to some other pieces of legislation in the labour field which we in this group have presented from time to time that the provinces were already giving us a lead and that the federal government was falling behind. That is the case with respect to some of the other matters we have placed before parliament at this session. So far as this item is concerned, the fact is that the provinces are rather slow in coming forward with appropriate legislation. I suggest that perhaps for once, instead of the federal government having to be prodded to get in step and having to be prodded to put on its statute books legislation akin to that which is on the statute books of most of the provinces, in this case the federal government might take the lead.
In other words, I am admitting that the picture in the provinces is not as progressive in this field of statutory holidays as labour generally and we in this party feel it should be. I find on reference to a document prepared by the Department of Labour entitled "Provincial Labour Standards", published under the authority of the Minister of Labour in December, 1955, that there are six provinces in which there is some legislation regarding statutory or public holidays.
Those six provinces, to take them in geographical order from east to west, are Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. However, in two of those provinces the only effect of the legislation regarding statutory or public holidays is that a certain number of holidays shall be observed. I might say with respect to these various provinces that have some legislation in this field that they vary as to the number of holidays declared to be public or statutory holidays. In some cases it is seven and in some it is eight, and various other figures are established in different provinces.
However, of the six provinces that have some kind of legislation respecting statutory or public holidays, there are four that make provision for what rates of pay employees are to receive if they are required to work on any of the statutory holidays set out in that provincial legislation. Those four, and again I take them in geographical order starting in the east, are Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Hon. members will note that I have now had to leave out Newfoundland and British Columbia, both of which were in the previous list of six which I gave. Those are the two whose

Industrial Relations
legislation merely prescribes that the holidays shall be observed. However, in the case of these four-Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-there are varying provisions as to the rates of pay that employees shall receive if they are required to work on statutory holidays.
It would be a confusing picture indeed if I tried to spell it all out, but I might just indicate that the rate varies from straight time to time and a half and perhaps more in some cases. There are also provisions in some instances for compensatory time off rather than extra pay. Some provinces make a distinction between one group of workers and another, and in some instances better protection is given to women than to others so far as statutory holidays are concerned. However, those four provinces go at least as far as to make some provision as to the rate of pay to be given to workers if they are required to work on statutory holidays.
There is only one province in the whole of Canada which takes the further step and requires that all workers shall receive pay for statutory holidays even though they do not work. I trust hon. members get the distinction. The three provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Nova Scotia make no provision for pay for statutory holidays if you do not work. They provide what you get if you do work, but Saskatchewan is the one province which is unique in this field because it has taken a further step and makes all three provisions; first, that there shall be observed certain statutory holidays; second, that those who work on those statutory holidays shall receive pay at an overtime rate; and third, that all employees, even those who do not work, shall receive pay at their regular rate for statutory holidays.

speechtext: This legislation would have no effect on the field normally covered by provincial statutes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Not at all. I thought I made it clear at the start that this bill, like other bills in this field, relates only to employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction. I am sure the hon. member will realize from the discussions we have had on other labour bills that every time we discuss labour conditions the question arises as to whether we are behind or in front of the provinces in that field. I have suggested that in some of the other fields the federal government is behind the provinces, and I am suggesting that in this field we are behind them as well. I am not saying that nothing has been done by the provinces, but very little has been done and it would not be very hard for the federal parliament to get out in front and give a lead.

It is my thought, and I am sure it is also the thought of some hon. members on the government side of the house, that if a lead were given in this matter by the federal parliament in connection with those employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction it might prompt some of the provinces to come along and do likewise.
There have been such instances. As a matter of fact the first jurisdiction in this country to pass legislation protecting the pension rights of workers against loss due to strikes was this federal parliament, which passed legislation in that field in 1948, after it had been asked for by some of us for many years. It was not very long after that step had been taken by the parliament of Canada in 1948 that that particular item of legislation was copied by a number of the provinces and pension rights are now pretty generally protected against loss due to strike or lockout, right across Canada. Similarly it is my conviction that if the federal parliament were to take a lead with respect to statutory holidays with pay it would set a goal at which the provinces might aim. I would hope that progress would be made in that field with a minimum of delay.
Before the hon. member for York-Scarbo-rough interjected his question I was coming to the conclusion of that part of my remarks in which 1 was trying to indicate the picture in the provinces, namely that something has been done but that much remains to be done in all provinces except one, namely the province of Saskatchewan, where eight holidays, the same eight that are spelled out in this bill, are declared to be statutory holidays and where it is declared also that those who do not work on those days shall receive their regular pay and that those who are required to work shall receive pay at overtime rates.
In addition to the interesting information which I gleaned from pages 8 and 9 of this departmental document entitled "Provincial Labour Studies", I also gleaned certain information from some interesting tables which the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour supplied to me. I am grateful to the minister's department for the receipt of this material. As a matter of fact I think I might take a moment to say that the people in the minister's department do a particularly good job in terms of collecting statistics and making them available. This may be a bit of a digression, but I want to say also that those who edit the Labour Gazette do a very good job of keeping people who are interested in labour matters informed on what is going on in the labour field. I suppose after having said that, a report of this debate should appear in the

next issue of the Labour Gazette, but that was not my purpose in putting in that word of compliment.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to a couple of the tables which appear in this collection of material I received relative to working conditions. One is table No. 29, which indicates the number of paid statutory holidays enjoyed by office employees in manufacturing establishments across Canada. What interested me is that the largest single group receiving statutory holidays, receive eight of them a year. Indeed, 61-1 per cent of office employees in manufacturing establishments, receive that nany paid statutory holidays a year.
It is difficult to get corresponding figures for hourly-paid workers, hence my reference to the position enjoyed by office workers. I suggest that it indicates something as to a goal which it might be desirable to achieve. The number who receive seven paid statutory holidays is 10-7 per cent, and those who receive nine or more is just about 20 per cent. In other words, the great bulk of that group of office workers who receive pay for statutory holidays, receive it for eight such holidays. It is on that basis that I suggest we are justified in asking this parliament to approve the principle of eight paid statutory holidays for all employees who come under the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament.
This same set of tables which I obtained from the minister's department deals with the question of rates of pay given to hourly-paid industrial workers when they do receive extra pay for working on statutory holidays. Hon. members will understand that when reference is made to hourly-paid workers who get extra pay for working on statutory holidays, we are talking not about something which they get by virtue of legislation but of something which they get by virtue in most cases of collective agreements. That would apply except for the provisions in the labour legislation in Saskatchewan. There is no other province in Canada in which the right to paid statutory holidays is protected by legislation.
Nevertheless, by virtue of collective agreements some paid statutory holidays are enjoyed by workers. One of the struggles in which the trade union movement is engaged all the time is to obtain that provision for more workers, and to get for those who enjoy that provision an increasing number of paid statutory holidays. In some agreements the number starts at four or five and gradually the number gets to six, seven or eight. But I am also interested in the question of the premium rates paid to those who
Industrial Relations
work on statutory holidays in manufacturing establishments, bearing in mind that most of these have been established by virtue of collective agreements between management and trade unions.
I find that according to table 23 in this group of tables I have in my hand, 9-4 per cent of those for whom there is a specified rate as to what they will get for working statutory holidays get time and a half as the premium rate. I find that 32-9 per cent get double time for working on statutory holidays, and that 39-1 per cent get more than double time. The table I have before me does not specify how much more, but in view of the fact that 32-9 per cent get double time and 39 [DOT] 1 per cent get more than double time, it seems to me that we are more than justified in asking in this bill that the rate of pay to those who are required to work on statutory holidays be their regular pay plus a premium rate of double time.
There are those, of course, who will probably produce in this debate the same argument that is produced every time we introduce legislation regarding labour matters, namely would it not be a good idea to leave this to collective bargaining? We have had that with regard to the check-off. We used to have it years ago when some of us were fighting for that other provision to which I referred, the protection of pension rights against loss due to strikes. We had it in the debate on Bill No. 211 a few weeks ago, and I suppose we shall get it again today. Frankly, I sometimes am surprised that members who put forward that kind of argument accept any labour legislation of any kind. After all, the logical conclusion of that sort of argument is to leave everything to collective bargaining, to leave everything to the struggle between management and labour.
Hon. members are fully aware of the importance of collective bargaining in labour relations and that importance is recognized by all parties in this house. But we have also recognized that step by step and stage by stage the point is reached where some things have to be protected, where pegs have to be established so the rights won by labour will not slip below those pegs.
Labour itself, the trade union movement, which defends the principle of collective bargaining and which is opposed to compulsory arbitration, nevertheless is continually seeking from the legislatures of the country and from this federal parliament legislation protecting certain of those hard-won rights. It is on that basis that labour has sought from parliament in years gone by laws to protect the right to organize and laws to

Industrial Relations
protect the practice of collective bargaining. It is on that basis that labour has sought measures such as I now lay before this house, namely annual vacations with pay and statutory holidays with pay for all workers in this country.
I hope the day is not far off when the argument that we must leave these things to .collective bargaining, which is another way of saying with respect to this sort of thing that we leave it to the struggle between the worker and the boss, will not be heard but rather that we will recognize that there are certain social rights that should be enjoyed by all the people of Canada. Though we ,do not have it by legislation in this country, .except in the one province of Saskatchewan, there are many Canadians today who because they are salaried employees, because they are monthly rate employees, because of collective agreements or for other reasons, enjoy statutory holidays with pay. There are statutory holidays. The provinces declare [DOT]that some of them should be observed and this parliament declares that certain others should be observed. Yet we leave a great many of our people without the benefit of knowing that when they enjoy those statutory holidays their pay for those days will continue.
I say again that this is an important year in Canadian labour history, with the birth of the new Canadian Labour Congress. I should hope that the parliament of Canada, even *before this session ends, might yet do something significant, something substantial, something that will recognize the birth of that new congress, something more than just words in the fine speeches that were made to the delegates when the congress was formed in Toronto in April. I suggest that one of these substantial, worth-while gestures that this parliament could make would be to pass these two bills. I mention them together because they are companion bills, the other one calling for two weeks' annual vacation with pay and this one calling for eight statutory holidays with pay for all workers in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has brought in for second reading the companion bill to Bill No. 211, and in presenting it to the house this afternoon he has presented with eloquence his appeal for those who come under the federal jurisdiction, that their conditions of work should be improved by act of this parliament. I know that it is always a very pleasant thing to sponsor something that one is sure a great many of the people directly concerned want to have done. Without a moment's hesitation I agree with him

that this and Bill No. 211 were among those matters that were discussed at the great Canadian Labour Congress held in Toronto a short time ago.
In spite of his remarks criticizing my habit of bringing up the virtue of collective bargaining on these matters, nevertheless I bring it up in this connection without making any apology for doing so. My comments must of necessity be along the same lines as those which I applied to Bill 211. This bill deals with a matter that is normally -and even more normally than what is asked for under Bill 211-a matter that is subject to collective bargaining. I stress again that the employees of industries which come under federal jurisdiction are in very truth highly organized unions. They are not of that weak and incapable nature that might be inferred from some of the words of my hon. friend, in that they require from time to time the bolstering of legislation by this parliament to uphold their hands. Their collective agreements have referred to items right across the board in the conditions of work and more particularly, as he has pointed out, in recent years to the items contained in this particular bill. For instance, there are the observance of certain statutory holidays, the pay that is to be given for those holidays and the premium pay for work that may be done if instructed to work on those holidays. In some industries, particularly the transportation or railway industries, the nature of the work calls for continuous operation of the service and rather specialized types of work scheduling have to be worked out. In order to do that, statutory holidays are dealt with in collective agreements	covering some	groups of
employees, and they are not a consideration of any great importance among other groups.
As examples of that I refer to the results of recent negotiations that have been going on. In the first example, statutory holidays were a very important factor in the collective bargaining during the last few months involving the 130,000 non-operating employees of the railways. On the other hand, in the dispute involving locomotive engineers statutory holidays were not a factor in the settlement arrived at, because in the view of the workers other things were more important than statutory holidays.
This indicates, I think, particularly in the transportation industries which come under federal jurisdiction, that there should be a flexibility to a degree not provided by this cover-all bill, in order to enable management and labour to work out a settlement. The bill makes no exception for any groups of workers whatsoever. The people who are

to come under it are listed in the usual fashion in the first part of the bill and include everybody coming within the jurisdiction of federal labour laws. I contend that the passing of the bill would do away with a necessary flexibility in working out their collective agreements.
When the two parties work out an agreement they look over all the working conditions that exist in the industry. One extra paid statutory holiday may be looked upon as as important or more important than a few cents in extra pay or vice versa, and for parliament to require by law a fixed number of holidays and the conditions of pay for those holidays would be to some extent an intervention in the collective bargaining process of a fairly serious nature in some industries.
In many parts of the world, of course, collective bargaining does not play the important part that it does in Canada. There the conditions of employment are laid down by the government in fairly rigid terms, but in Canada we hold the view that the role of labour legislation that deals with economic issues, as this bill does, is to provide for a basic standard. I contend, as was clear in the summary of statistics and reports given by my hon. friend, that Bill No. 441 goes quite some distance beyond a basic standard in this year 1956.
Some very important gains have been made in this field in recent years, but even with the gains that have been made the terms set out in the bill go beyond what labour law administrators in the provincial or federal jurisdiction consider to be a basic standard. There is some evidence that unorganized workers have shared in the gains and improvements that have been made in recent years. Out of about 380,000 employees coming under federal jurisdiction, some 90 per cent now receive some paid statutory holidays. As my hon. friend said, about 40 per cent of the workers receive eight or more statutory holidays and most of the remainder receive six or seven. Therefore, while my hon. friend may not be away out in the vanguard with regard to the total number of holidays, I do contend that with respect to the pay for such holidays, the overtime rate, with the exception of one province, the province of Saskatchewan, to which he referred no jurisdiction reaches the high point which my hon. friend has reached in the bill.
I should like to refer again to the transportation industry in this year 1956. I am going to take four examples of settlements. Three are in the transportation industry and one happens to be in the radio industry. Employees of radio station CKLW, Windsor,
Industrial Relations
achieved seven statutory holidays with pay through collective bargaining. With regard to the operating railway employees, the locomotive engineers to whom I referred a moment ago, the statutory holiday factor played no important part in the settlement of their dispute. In the case of the C.P.R. dining car employees' dispute, the employees had four statutory holidays prior to this year and they will have seven after this year under the new agreement. In the case of the non-operating railway employees' dispute, prior to 1956 they had gained five statutory holidays through collective bargaining. In the recent settlement they gained a sixth statutory holiday in 1956 and a seventh commencing in 1957. That settlement affected about 130,000 workers.
These four settlements of recent date indicate the great variety of desires on the part of workers in reaching their collective agreements, and the great variety of opinion that exists on the topic covered by the bill. If the provisions of the bill were made law and came into effect on the 1st day of September next, the industries to which I have referred and others to which I have not referred would have to adjust their hard-sought and hard worked-out agreements to conform to the terms of this new legislation, and it would certainly create a situation that I would not want to be a party to bringing about.
I made some reference to the situation as it exists in the provinces. I have no dispute whatsoever with the interpretation that has been placed upon the information by my hon. friend. He has given a fair summary of the situation, though I do contend that as far as this matter is concerned we should not be in the position of prodding the provinces. If we feel it is essential within our own jurisdiction, we should do it on that account only. We should not set ourselves up as advisers, and should not give ourselves the special task of prodding the provinces to do something they do not want to do.
Bill No. 441 provides that there are to be eight specified public holidays for which an employee is to receive his regular wages even if he does not work. The sponsor made that very clear. If he does work he is to receive his regular wages plus a sum equal to twice that amount. In other words he will receive triple wages for that particular statutory holiday if he works. In the light of what we know about collective agreement provisions and provincial legislation, it is clear that this is well beyond anything we have at the present time.
As to the principle of the bill, the question of whether or not legislation to deal

Industrial Relations
with the payment of wages on statutory holidays is necessary, I can tell my hon. friend that my department will continue to study that matter. The possible need for legislation such as the bill presents will be looked into. I welcome the fact that the hon. member has brought the matter before the house at the present time, but if it comes to a vote I shall not be able to support the bill for the reasons I have given.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), as I always do when we come to the discussion of topics of this nature. As he himself indicated, some of the arguments he advanced had a familiar ring.
I may say at once that, as far as 1 am concerned, I find myself heartily in support of the bill which has been introduced in the house by the member for Winnipeg North Centre. When we consider a bill of this kind or a bill which has been described as a companion to this one and on which we had discussion a short time ago, I feel that those of us who are members of the federal parliament of Canada have a responsibility to think a little bit about the kind or nature of society in which we are moving in Canada, the kind of society in which we hope our children and children's children will find themselves able to live.
I am not able to boast of a great number of years as far as my own span of life is concerned, but even in the relatively short period over which I am able to look back I think I can honestly say that I have seen quite a transformation in the attitude which a great many people in Canada take toward the kind of conditions under which the Canadian people should live and work. I agree that in the legislative field we cannot advance beyond certain reasonable minimums in the standards that are set by legislation; we cannot attempt to achieve the impossible by legislation. Nevertheless when one thinks of the tremendous change that has taken place in our ability to produce goods and services in the last 10, 15, 20 or 25 years, if one assesses the matter fairly I think one must come to the point of admitting that a proposal of the nature of that advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in this bill is not beyond the realm of reasonableness.
The minister suggested that there were grounds on which we could concern ourselves with the setting of certain minimum standards. As far as I am concerned, I would be prepared to argue here or anywhere else that the proposals which are contained in

this bill do not go beyond the setting of reasonable minimum conditions which, in this day and age, all Canadian citizens should, by right, be able to enjoy.
It may be perfectly true, as the minister says, that this legislation in the federal field would affect only a relatively small percentage, those coming within federal labour jurisdiction. If that is the case, even in part, I would submit that fact in itself is an argument in favour of the passage of this bill. I would agree with him that it is not particularly the duty of this parliament to try to force the provinces into the position of being obliged to pass certain legislation. I am quite sure that was not what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had in mind when he made some reference to that aspect of the situation. We all recognize the fact that in their own jurisdictions the provinces are supreme. However, I would suggest that there is nothing to prevent us taking upon our own responsibility, in the field of social legislation, action which we consider to be for the welfare of the Canadian people as far as we have legislative concern for it, and to hope that our example may be considered worth copying.
It is not a matter of telling anybody what to do or of intimidation. It is merely a matter, under certain circumstances perhaps, of setting a desirable lead which may be followed by legislators in our provinces or in other parts of the world. I believe that legislation which has come into being in most of the democratic countries from time to time has been materially influenced by what has been done by other powers. I believe that we learn-and I think rightly so- from what the parliament of the United Kingdom does or from what the parliaments in the Scandinavian countries do or, generally speaking, from what is done in parliaments in countries where the people have a somewhat similar outlook to that prevailing in this country on matters of this kind.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that in the time that remains, I will not have the opportunity of saying all that I perhaps might like to say in this phase of the debate. I feel that the basic principles of the bill were set forth quite completely in the introductory speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. From a study of the subject matter of the bill itself and from what he has said in his speech I feel that the members of this house, after a little reflection, will perhaps come to realize that this is a measure which should receive the stamp of approval of this parliament at an early date.

committee rose at five o'clock I was dealing with the present state of the air force auxiliary units and posing the question why, with all the increasing demands for air transport facilities, heightened by the new emphasis on an airborne army and the necessity for mobility of troops; and I think the last point I was raising was the situation relating to the presence of Canadian troops in Europe, who would be faced with the necessity of rapid evacuation if hostilities ever developed on the continent of Europe. We had some discussion about this last night, in which it was suggested that plans for the rapid evacuation of those Canadian service personnel and their dependents are still in the process of formulation, and we are diminishing our air transport facilities. No doubt any comprehensive plan would require the use of air force transport facilities.
Supply-National Defence
To bring these remarks to a conclusion in the form of some concrete questions, I should like to ask the minister why it is that with these increasing demands for air force transport we seem to be diminishing our transport facilities rather than enlarging them. This is the case with the auxiliary squadrons as well as with our regular transport squadrons, or it would seem to me to be so. On May 10 of this year I received an answer to a question about the number and kind of aircraft operated by transport command. Unfortunately I was not too specific with my questions and in reply to the following question-
What aircraft are operated by the H.C.A.F. transport command?
-I got merely a listing of the types of aircraft, such as Lancaster, North Star, C-119, and so forth. I am wondering whether the minister can complete the answer at this time by indicating the number of aircraft of each type that are operational with transport command at the present time? I think it would help to make the answer much more meaningful than it is in the present form.
Finally, returning to the main burden of my presentation at this time, I find it difficult, with the increasing need for transport facilities, to understand why the decision has been taken to disband a squadron as efficient as 424, which has expressed its desire to serve in any capacity. I understand in its representations it particularly mentioned that it would be happy as a transport squadron to supply light transport which would meet the need for a mobile striking force which could stand in an emergency as a unit of civil defence activity, or which could serve in any general role in a transport capacity.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Middlesex East in which he presented the case of 420 London squadron to the minister. That squadron is not being disbanded; it is being reorganized as a radar unit. Again I have had some contact with the personnel of that squadron; I know it is fully operational as a flying unit, and it is their wish that they remain operational in a flying capacity. It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that with the rapidly increasing demands for transport facilities the reserve squadrons, instead of being decreased in flying duties at this time, might well be expanded.
One reason the minister gave in justifying the reorganization of those particular auxiliary units was economy. I hardly think that is a justifiable contention, because as I look at page 338 of the estimates and consider that for the past 10 years the reserve

Supply-Naticnial Defence squadrons have been regarded as the backbone of Canadian defence, I think we have been receiving that protection at extremely reasonable cost. Compare it, for example, with the expenditure of $24 million for experimental work on the guided missile we were discussing this afternoon, the "Velvet Glove". Mr. Chairman, I can assure the hon. member that the decisions we have taken with regard to the reserve air force, as I have already said, were taken after a great deal of study, a great deal of consideration and after consultation with the senior officers of all the squadrons whom we called in some time ago.
The reserve air force has given very fine service throughout its history. We have come to the point in defence where we have to look for economies and to consider the results obtained in relation to the moneys spent. One of the things that became evident as we made a study of this problem was that it was very expensive to operate air auxiliary squadrons in places where there were no other air force flying activities, and particularly in those places where there was no other flying activity, as in the case of Hamilton where, as I have already said in the house, it cost upwards of $1 million to provide an airfield for flying for the pilots and air crew of the auxiliary squadron on week ends.
Now, having come to that conclusion-and 1 do not want to go into all the details of the financial aspects-the question was how could we utilize the services of the persons in the auxiliary squadron most usefully, having regard to any other air force activities in the community and having regard to the territory from which they might draw and the number of people we might expect to continue active in their services? And here I would like to interject, because I do not think there should be any secret about it, that the Sabre jet is not being put into certain auxiliary air squadrons as a major item in the defence of the country. The objections which were quoted by my hon. friend still obtain; Sabres were given to six of the twelve squadrons because they were located in areas where the population was great enough to support squadron activities.
Now, the situation was different in respect of each of the several squadrons. Take the


Winnipeg squadron for example. Navigational training is a very important factor. A very expensive school is maintained at Winnipeg to train regular force air crew in navigation. It was felt therefore that the auxiliary squadron there could very usefully participate in training navigators.
As regards the Hamilton squadron, I have mentioned the fact that it was located at an airport which we had to operate solely for the purpose of maintaining week end flying for an auxiliary squadron. As far as London is concerned there was no air defence control and warning unit stationed there and I can assure the hon. member that the assistance of auxiliary personnel there in this role will be very important to the R.C.A.F. It was felt that having regard to the set-up with which the squadron in London could be associated, it could very usefully serve in the role of an aircraft warning and control.
In regard to Calgary, for various reasons it was felt that a small transport training squadron could be usefully located there in addition to other activities being carried on. They were all considered together and then each one was considered separately. These decisions which have been taken represent as I have already said, a good deal of study by the air force, who should be expected to know the most useful functions the auxiliaries can perform from now on, in the foreseeable future. It was with great reluctance that we made the changes we did make, but they were not made haphazardly and without consideration. As regards the general set-up, we will still have six auxiliary squadrons flying. The other six will assume other duties which to the air force seem useful and necessary.
The hon. member asked, with regard to the transport squadrons, the types of planes we have and the numbers of each type. I have them here by squadrons, with the number of aircraft listed. At No. 426 squadron, based at Dorval, there are 12 North Stars. At No. 412 squadron, based at Rockcliffe, there are nine Dakotas, three Expeditors, two North Stars, and one C-5. At No. 435 squadron, based at Edmonton, there are eight C-119's. At No. 4 transport, based at Trenton, there are three North Stars, three C-119's, three Dakotas and one Expeditor. At the R.C.A.F. station, Lachine, there are two Expeditors. At the R.C.A.F. station, Goose Bay, there is one Dakota and one Otter. At the R.C.A.F. station, Churchill, there is one Otter. At No. 436 squadron, Dorval, there are six C-119's. At 108 flight at Rockcliffe, which is a helicopter flight, there are 22 helicopters.

I quoted the total figure of $4| million which, in the light of today's astronomical expenditures, particularly for air defence, is a mere bagatelle. That, of course, is for the reserve only, and it is a mere trifle as compared with the whole defence expenditure.
Referring again to the reply I received to my question of May 10, I inquired as to the number of multi-engine aircraft that would be required to make a fully equipped infantry brigade air portable. The reply was it would depend on the type of aircraft used, of course, but an example could be given. If the C-119 aircraft were used the number required would be 148. As I look at the number of C-119's in service with the transport command at the present time they come to 17 or 18 aircraft, which means we would be short some 100 planes in meeting the requirements for air-lifting one infantry brigade.
I said at the beginning of my remarks concerning the functions of auxiliary squadrons that we have had constant changes of policy in regard to reserve squadron activities. In the first instance they were responsible for the total defence of Canada. We criticized that concept and now, as I said in my remarks of yesterday, I believe it seems that we are beginning to minimize the effectiveness of auxiliary squadrons.
I do not think Canada has sufficient funds to maintain an adequate air defence force on a full time permanent basis. The minister has announced that that is the essential function of Canada's role in the defence of North America; and if we are going to justify the expenditures for the three radar lines we must have adequate aircraft to back up the billion dollar expenditure. I think the total expenditure for the "Pinetree", mid-Canada and D.E.W. lines comes to about $1 billion.

While I have defended the radar policy in this house to a limited extent, I know it has been under severe criticism from rather responsible and authoritative sources in Canada as well as in the United States. If we are going to minimize the function of the auxiliary squadrons by arbitrarily disbanding and reorganizing as we have in recent days, it is certainly not going to have a very stimulating and beneficial effect on morale.
We have sufficient difficulty as it is interesting young Canadians in devoting their time to the defence of the country on a permanent basis. I do not think it is in the best interests of the over-all defensive role that Canada is obliged to assume in the defence of North America to allow the pendulum to swing from one extreme where we are dependent on the auxiliary for our total defence to the other extreme. To ensure that materials and equipment transferred by Canada as mutual aid do go to the nation or nations able to use it to the best advantage of NATO as a whole, offers are made initially through the standing group or the NATO secretariat. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, when I retreated from the position of quarterback in the last debate I did not realize I was going to be the fullback in this debate commencing at 20 minutes past nine.
I would like to say in the beginning that there seems to be considerable concern about the situation which confronts our aircraft industry in this country today. I think that concern involves not only the question of employment but it involves as well the question of the maintenance of adequate facilities. In times of emergencies it also involves the maintenance of qualified trained technical personnel to meet such emergencies.
In the discussion which took place in connection with the defence estimates I questioned the minister along certain lines, because I felt quite sure there would be some question raised at a later date as to whether my remarks referred to the Department of Defence Production or whether in fact they referred to defence or transport. I said at that time, and I still feel, that if we have to cross these lines this seems a logical place for such a discussion, because I think everyone in the house would look to the leadership of the Minister of Defence Production to bring about any liaison that is required to deal with problems of this kind.
First of all let me say this. I cannot accept the theory as I heard it expressed in one way or another by the minister that the government has no responsibility in connection with employment in defence industries. I have heard him say, for example, that A. V. Roe is a private company, that they manage their own affairs and he does not interfere.

Supply-Defence Production
It may be true that in many industries the government does not have to play any particular role, as there may be possibilities of diversification of one sort and another. That would apply even to industries within the aircraft industry. A manufacturer of electronic items in connection with control apparatus for the CF-100 may also be making hi-fi sets. But when you get down to the companies actually involved in the production of aircraft you find it is most difficult for them to diversify, to manufacture other things which will keep their production lines rolling.
This industry certainly has reached fairly important proportions in so far as our total production capacity is concerned. I think the minister said that at the present time the aircraft industry ranks ninth in value of production and third in employment. That is readily understandable when we realize the various projects being carried on at the present time.
There is the CF-105 being manufactured by A. V. Roe at Malton. There is the continuing production of the CF-100 with its various marks, the latest being mark VI. We have the CL-28, which is the Britannia maritime reconnaissance plane, a revised version of a British transport plane which is to go into production at Canadair. We have the CS2F anti-submarine aircraft being manufactured by de Havilland at Toronto. There is the development by Orenda of the PS-13 turbojet engine, which gives indications of having the most powerful thrust of any engine in the field today. There is the R18-220 engine to be used in the CS2F, which I understand is being manufactured under licence. As far as the engines for the CL-28 are concerned, they are being purchased. The minister stated that the quantity required was not large enough for us to become involved in manufacturing, that it was cheaper to buy.
One of the chief concerns today is the indication of a slow-down in the production line at A.V. Roe at Malton. I said this afternoon, and I think I may be permitted to repeat, that this could be caused probably by any one of three reasons. It may be that the CF-105 program is not advancing rapidly enough. After having inspected the facilities and seen the aircraft my personal feeling is that it will not come along just as fast as was expected, but it seems to be making very rapid progress. I would say that any slow-down there is not the result of any failure on the part of the company to go along with the development of this very radical plane.
That leaves a couple of more ideas why there may be a stretchout in this program.

It may be that there are not enough men being induced to join the air and ground crews of the air force. That is a very serious situation and is one with which the Minister of National Defence will have to grapple. According to the information given to the house there is every indication that this may be a serious problem in the future. It may be that one reason there are not enough men coming along to man these fighter planes is that we are not fitting them basically to fly the type of plane they would be called upon to fly in peacetime. They may be expecting to get full training in the armed forces to equip them to do that job.
I think there is real reason for concern over this slow-down. There is nothing to fill in during what might be called the bust period in connection with the wartime type of production. It seems to me that there is a responsibility upon the government to work out the solution of that problem in industry, especially when it is almost impossible for the industry to diversify their production lines.
What is the result of the failure of the government to accept responsibility for looking into this? What is the result of the lack of continuity on the production line? One thing we can be sure of, the taxpayer is the one who is going to pay. Notwithstanding the information we have had here, notwithstanding the indication that there are various types of contracts which may be entered into -I have heard them referred to as a cost-plus plan, a target price with incentive features and a negotiated price-there can be only one result, and that is that the taxpayer must pay more money for the individual item which is bought. I say that notwithstanding the types of contracts we have heard about, that will be the result. At page 14 of the report of the department we find the following:
A continuing increase in production efficiency resulted in decreased costs for the CF-100. Further development of this aircraft was undertaken during the year to obtain more powerful armament, greater altitude, and improved manoeuvrability. Series 11 and 14 Orenda jet engines for both the Sabre and CF-100 continued to be produced satisfactorily, but at a reduced rate reflecting the reduction in aircraft output.
Similarly we find this statement by the Minister of National Defence at page 6124 of Hansard of July 18:
Similarly, in the case of the CF-100, development costs prior to the production of the first plane were given last year as being around $122 million. The current unit cost, with spares, is a little over $700,000.
The minister went on to deal with the Sabre and his words there were as follows:
Although we made a number of improvements in the Sabre, our aircraft industry also managed

to work out substantial production economies and the current unit cost of a Sabre mark VI, complete with spares, is now about $340,000.
There is one point that is missed. The A. V. Roe plant in Toronto is set up and equipped to produce 25 planes a month of the type we are talking about. When the production is cut down to 10, whether it is a negotiated price or a target price with incentive features, you are still going to pay more money for your plane. A formula has been worked out to cover the over-all picture which indicates that $1 must be spent on the actual production of the plane as against $1.35 for administration and general overhead. That is considered a good ratio if you are producing at your full production rate. But if you cut your production rate down from 25 to 10 then obviously you change the ratio in so far as your administrative expenses are concerned as compared with the actual money spent in producing the plane.
The Minister of National Defence said today that a plane of this type now costs about $700,000. It is conceivable that because of this cut-back in production we are paying a few hundred dollars more for a plane than if the production line were in full use. Of course there is the further problem of employment, and I think it is a very serious one. I have here a copy of the Globe and Mail of Friday, June 29, 1956, with the heading:
"Breach of Faith".
Union Criticizes Howe Over Malton Layoffs.
We might read this and we can see exactly what the situation is in connection with employment in a case of this kind. It says:
The federal government yesterday was charged with a breach of faith following an announcement that an estimated 500 workers will be laid off at Avro aircraft's Malton plant. The charge was contained in a telegram sent to defence production minister Howe, whose departmental request that the production rate of CF-100 jet interceptors be stretched out, resulted in the lay-offs. . . .
In January, 1955, the company laid off 1,100 workers, cutting the monthly production of CF-100's by 40 per cent. Three months later, another 1,000 workers were given notice of a gradual layoff.
It is no wonder there is a feeling that it may be impossible to maintain that type of production line to which the minister has referred as avoiding the troughs or periods of low activity.
There were attempts in connection with this particular company to produce other types of aircraft, and apparently they did not meet with the entire approval of the minister. I know that during the course of this debate reference was made to the production of the jet liner. I think the minister said that was a closed book and need not refer to that again, but it seemed to me that the indications from his answers were 67509-398
Supply-Defence Production that it was not so much the start of the Korean war that had resulted in the closing of this production line, which I think might have been the salvation from the standpoint of maintaining a clean-cut through-put in connection with that production line, but the fact that he had decided that the plane was not going to live up to expectations. As a matter of fact it might be wise to see what he said about it:
My hon. friend referred to our first attempt at building a jet liner. It is true we had the manufacturing capacity and we wished to keep a nucleus staff working at Malton. Therefore we undertook to produce a jet passenger plane. We brought it to the prototype stage; and while it is true it flew, there was everything wrong with it. It had to carry sand bags in the tail to fly properly.
Not according to reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I get my reports and the hon. member gets his. I have to trust mine and I am sure his are not accurate. Nevertheless, we spend the money allocated to us for specific projects, and we get reports which we believe are accurate. It so happened that the Comet was being developed at the time, and although the Comet did not come into production until two or three years later there was nothing encouraging about the results of that prototype at Avro on which we had spent $6-6 million.
I thought all along that there was an indication that we interrupted this particular production because of a crisis in the Korean war but, if I am to believe this type of evidence, it was because the minister had no faith in the aircraft itself. But I want to tell you this, that apparently the company did not feel that way, and the people who worked on the project did not feel that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I ask my
hon. friend a question? Why did the company not keep on with the jet liner? We did not stop it. We were paying 75 per cent of the cost as a joint venture, and we said we would not contribute our 75 per cent any more. We did not stop the company. It was their jet liner, and they could have carried on.

I should think the minister would know the answer to that very easily. He happens to have under his control, as one of the many features, Trans-Canada Air Lines. If he says he does not like the plane at Malton I am sure he is not going to like it anywhere else, and the company would have been very foolish under those circumstances to put any more funds into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I thought they had customers for it all over the United States. That was your statement the other day.

Supply-Defence Production

It was not my
statement, but I should think that anyone producing here would have a basic loyalty to a Canadian product, and I think in this particular case that was lacking in the minister. The article in the Toronto Telegram of June 30, 1956, says:
Company Denies Charging Politics Grounded Plane
Avro aircraft officials still think their jet liner is a wonderful airplane. But defence production minister Howe today insisted that the prototype "was hopeless".
At the same time Avro vice president Fred T. Smye denied any Avro official had claimed there was political interference on the jet liner project, abandoned in 1950 to put the company's full production weight behind the CF-100 fighter.
"You would have to be out of your mind to say that," said Mr. Smye.
I suppose you would if you were dealing with this government every day of the week.
Mr. Howe said in a telephone interview that his inspectors had told him the prototype, Canada's first commercial-type jet aircraft, had not passed inspection and never would.
"That plane was hopeless," said the minister.
Mr. Howe told the House of Commons yesterday the "plane had to carry sand in the tail to fly."
Avro argued the sand was ballast in the wings to make up the weight of equipment not installed in the test model.
"Sand in the tail-sand in the wings," said Mr. Howe. "Inspectors told me they would never pass the plane. Besides, the whole thing is a dead duck so why bring it up."
Avro, aided by an $8 million government loan, built the prototype in 1949. However, there were no bidders for the first jet air liner built in North America.
Mr. Howe said lack of buyer interest and increased production of CF-100 jets for the Korean war were other factors which had killed the jetliner project.
Avro feels Mr. Howe should regard the plane more highly. "It is still a wonderful airplane." the company said.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: May I interject that the abuse I am getting from my hon. friend and the Toronto press for stopping the building of an airplane in Toronto does not compare in any way with the abuse I got for carrying one on in the city of Montreal. I may say that in those days the Globe and Mail knew how to write bitter editorials and they certainly gave us the full dose. I fought the Conservative party all through an election for trying to blame the government for building an airplane, so I guess I can take with some equanimity any mild abuse my hon. friend can hand out for stopping the building of an airplane.
If I have abused the minister I will say that it is the first time I have done so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: No.
The minister is sensitive.

It may be that I have hit a sensitive area for the first time. It may be that I myself have a feeling of loyalty to a plant in an area with which I am closely identified, which has made me say the things I have, but I still think they are very important. Although I did not take part as a candidate in the campaign the minister mentioned, I think he is a little off base when he says that we argued over the efficiency or stability of an aircraft. I think the major issue at that time, and apparently people still do not see it, was the machinations of the Electric Boat Company and the sale of the plant in Montreal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Oh, no; it was the North Star aircraft.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You were too young to know what the debate was about. It was not about that at all.
That is what it was about, but you tried to make it appear that it was not about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will read you some clippings. It was whether or not the North Star was safe.

Time.
67509-398i
Supply-Defence Production

It may be time but I will certainly have plenty of opportunity to continue. There are now 454 such planes. I am not going to tell you all about those planes. You can read the return for yourself. However, there were none manufactured in Canada. They were imported from Great Britain, Italy and chiefly from the United States. It might also be of interest to hon. members to know that there were only 39 that were new and 129 were used. That gives a fairly clear indication of the position of civil aircraft in Canada. It gives a fairly clear indication that there is and will continue to be an opportunity to utilize the production lines of our aircraft factories in building transports of the type we can make use of in the northern areas of this country.
Someone may say that 148 planes are not very many. I can tell you that in the Avro brief before the Gordon commission it was stated that they could successfully develop and build on an economic basis and compete anywhere if they had an order for 100 planes. I am not going to read that to you tonight, sir-
Your time is up.
We have a new timekeeper.
Your time has never started.

He has the
voice of a major league umpire and about as many brains. The Avro brief before the Gordon commission has this to say about civil possibilities:
Military aviation is a matter of survival. Civil aviation is primarily a matter of economics in its role in the growth of our economy and in keeping pace with other countries in commerce and industry. To maintain her position as a major trading nation and to continue the development of national resources Canada particularly will need commercial aircraft of the most advanced types m use anywhere. . . . Also there is one Canadian area in which aviation stands virtually alone-the north.
Further on the brief has this to say:
The great need in this northern push, even today, is an all-purpose aircraft designed to meet northern conditions-rigorous climate, long ranges, remote airports with short runways. In addition to its commercial role it would have a military function as a troop and supply transport. A transport of this kind would be ideal on the D.E.W. line and other radar line projects.
As for production costs the brief has this to say, and here is the comparison:
As for production costs, the CF-100 and the Orenda, which are as good if not better than anything available elsewhere, have been delivered at prices below what we would have had to pay elsewhere. The CF-100 costs substantially less than a comparable United States aircraft while the Orenda is several thousand dollars cheaper

Supply-Defence Production than its United States counterpart. This is on the basis of production of more than 400 CF-100's and over 3,000 Orendas.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall reply very briefly. It was stated that Canada had not built civilian aircraft. Canada is building civilian aircraft and a good many of them. The de Havilland company, with works within a few miles of Malton, are building civilian aircraft. They are getting civilian orders and they have not asked for any government help in designing these planes or, at least, very minor government help.
The hon. gentleman suggests that nobody can design a plane here unless the government supplies the money. I think that is something that is slightly out of tune with the practice in any country of the world that I know about. I do not know of any country where the designer of a civil plane goes to the government to get money to bring it into production. However, I will say this to the hon. gentleman, in spite of the lay-offs to which he refers. The lay-offs are purely a matter of protecting the great body of labour in the plant by stretching out the program to cover a gap between one type of production and another. There are over 10,000 people working in Avro at Malton. There are some
5,000	people working for de Havilland at Malton. I do not know what the number is at Canadair in Montreal but I should think it is about 8,000.
My hon. friend may be optimistic enough to think that force can be carried through the years and that we can keep that labour force building aircraft in normal times. I hope he is right. I am doing my best to hold the line steady and to produce the planes that seem to be required to meet the present-day situation. Anything I do is along that line. He says that I say I have no responsibility for aircraft. I do not go into a privately-owned plant and tell them how many men they need. However, I try to allocate such work as the government has in such a way that we can maintain reasonably steady employment. When we move out of a period of build-up of production of aircraft into a period when that build-up has been completed, I do not know of any way in which you can hold the maximum staff required for the build-up in order to carry on operations to meet normal requirements of a military type in this country. If the hon. member knows, I think perhaps he had better give me the pattern, because I thought we were doing quite a scientific job in meeting military demands, cutting down as the requirements are cut down and maintain-
ing reasonably steady employment in our aircraft plants.

As there are only about five minutes left, perhaps I might ask the minister if he really compares the development and manufacture here of aircraft of the Beaver or Otter type with the type of aircraft which we have seen imported here in quantities-it looks like a couple of hundred-over the period of the last year to year and a half? Does he know of any comparable aircraft of the type of which I am speaking which has been built in the United States without assistance from the government in its original development as a military aircraft?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do indeed; many of them. The DC-6 and the DC-7, Douglas planes, were built without military assistance. The hon. member talks about jet transport aircraft now being built. As a matter of fact T.C.A. has an order for four or five. That aircraft will cost between five and six million dollars. It is being built on civilian orders and without any government assistance whatever. I could go on and mention others such as the Lockheed Lone Star, which is a turbo-prop plane being built to fill civilian orders. As a matter of fact, in the case of the stratocruiser-that is the Boeing strato-cruiser-that was built as a civilian plane and was later taken over by the army and developed as a tanker to supply jet aircraft in the air. But there are more modern planes brought into production in the United States on civilian orders than there are adaptations of military planes.

The minister, of course, would admit that in about three of the five instances he gave the aircraft in question has been a subsequent development. When he talks about the DC-6, that is a line of aircraft which was developed, I think, during the last war.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, no.
It may be that they comprise the next step along the line, but certainly they got assistance in the first instance in order to get into production.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. I should like to make a statement on this matter, but as it is practically ten o'clock I should simply like at this moment to ask a question about item 85. I notice that telephones and telegrams are down from $175,000 to $130,000. I am just wondering why.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The result of an economy drive put on in the department.
That is the first one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The most recent of many.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We keep whittling away every year. Perhaps you have noticed that our estimates are being cut down every year. They have been cut down every year since 1953.

That is wonderful. I am just noticing an item of a somewhat similar type, namely office stationery, supplies and equipment, which is up from $190,000 to $204,500. I am just wondering, if they are really economy-minded, why they should be cutting down so considerably with regard to telephones and telegrams and then increasing with respect to office stationery, supplies and equipment. Does that mean they are cutting down on telephones and telegrams and writing more letters? I think many government departments should do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the answer, yes; plus a slight increase in the cost of fine paper.
